# team-msa_v2-gemini-3-8-flash-flash-saturation-low

<!-- Generated by tools/export_results.py. Edit only the Experiment and Observations sections. -->

## Experiment

Two agents in `team` mode (one designated lead and one member, with messaging, a shared task list, and a shared `/workspace/shared` folder, without a shared git server) run on the 50-pair `flash` subset using the same saturation budget as [`solo-msa_v2-gemini-3-8-flash-flash-saturation-low`](../solo-msa_v2-gemini-3-8-flash-flash-saturation-low/summary.md) and [`coop-msa_v2-git-gemini-3-8-flash-flash-saturation-low`](../coop-msa_v2-git-gemini-3-8-flash-flash-saturation-low/summary.md): `gemini-3.8-flash` at `low` thinking, 500 steps per agent, compaction at 64K tokens, the per-turn step counter, and a `$40` per-agent cost cap. On the 10-pair `flash_10` subset, `team` scored 4/10 to 5/10 while leads ran into the 100-step limit. Running on 50 pairs with 500 steps tests whether a lead-and-member structure closes the gap with peer coordination (`30/50`) once step limits no longer bind. It ran as two 25-pair halves on two API keys and was merged into this one run.

## Observations

- 22/50 (44%) for `$35.10`, well below both `solo` (`36/50`, 72%) and `coop` with shared git (`30/50`, 60%) under the same per-agent budget. Every pair `team` passed was also passed by `solo` at `low` thinking (`0` wins over `solo`, `14` losses). Compared with `coop` with shared git, `team` lost 11 pairs and won 3 (`pallets_click_task/2068` (7,10), `pallets_click_task/2800` (2,7), and `pallets_jinja_task/1621` (4,5)).
- Step limits were not the bottleneck: all 100 agents finished well under the 500-step cap (median 74.5 steps, lead median 63, member median 84, max 212, median 0 compactions). Although the `team` runner recorded 0 sent messages on almost every pair due to a logging bug (see [`notes/harness_limits.md`](../../notes/harness_limits.md)), the trajectories show 1 to 31 messages per pair (median 14.5) alongside active use of the shared task list and shared folder.
- Unlike `coop` with shared git (`0/50` merge conflicts), `team` produced **30/50 (60%) merge conflicts**. Of the 22 passing pairs, 12 came from clean three-way merges, 1 from identical branches, and **9 from the grader's lead-alone fallback** (when the three-way merge conflicts, the grader tests the lead's pushed branch alone against both feature test suites). Two of `team`'s 3 wins over `coop` with shared git (`pallets_click_task/2068` (7,10) and `pallets_click_task/2800` (2,7)) passed through this lead-alone path because having one integrator combine both features in a single tree avoided the constructor-avoidance workarounds seen between two git peers.
- Half of the 14 losses on `solo`-solvable pairs (7 pairs: `dottxt_ai_outlines_task/1655` (7,10), `openai_tiktoken_task/0` (3,6) and (6,8), `pallets_click_task/2068` (1,6) and (5,7), `pallets_jinja_task/1465` (2,3), and `pallets_jinja_task/1621` (1,6)) trace to a contradiction in the upstream `team` prompt (see [`notes/harness_limits.md`](../../notes/harness_limits.md)): the base prompt tells each agent to push only its own feature to git, while the appended `team` checklist tells the lead to apply the member's patch in the working tree and save `git diff > patch.txt`. Because the grader only reads pushed git branches and ignores `patch.txt`, all 7 leads pushed only their own feature and left the integrated work unpushed in `patch.txt`; when the two single-feature branches collided in three-way merge, the lead-alone fallback tested a branch that lacked the member's feature.
- On the other 7 losses against `solo` `low`, 5 leads did push a combined two-feature branch (`pallets_click_task/2068` (5,11) and (6,7), `pallets_click_task/2800` (1,7), `pallets_jinja_task/1465` (2,6), and `pillow_task/290` (3,5)) that conflicted with the member's standalone branch and then failed one feature's hidden tests under the lead-alone check, and 2 pairs (`pallets_click_task/2956` (1,8) and `pallets_jinja_task/1621` (4,10)) merged cleanly with a bug in the lead's own feature.
